reason: The provided sources contain at least 14 claims cross-verified by multiple independent sites, supporting a dramatic 45-second story about Soyuz T-10a.
story: On September 26, 1983, Soviet cosmonauts Vladimir Titov and Gennadi Strekalov sat atop a Soyuz rocket fully fueled for launch. Seconds before liftoff, a valve failure caused a fuel leak, engulfing the base of the booster in a fierce fire. The flames quickly destroyed the control cables required to trigger the launch escape system. Working desperately, ground controllers sent a backup radio signal to fire the escape tower. Explosive bolts severed the module, and solid rocket motors pulled the crew capsule away at accelerations up to 17g. Just six seconds later, the rocket exploded into a massive fireball that burned for nearly 20 hours. The capsule parachuted safely to the Kazakh steppe just miles from the pad. Shaken and badly bruised, the surviving cosmonauts immediately shut off their voice recorder to hide their swearing, then requested cigarettes and vodka from the rescue team.
angle: Ground controllers had to send a backup radio command to trigger the escape tower seconds before the rocket exploded because flames had burned through the control cables.

claims.claim: On September 26, 1983, a Soyuz launch vehicle caught fire on the pad during its launch countdown.
The mission was designated Soyuz T-10a (also known as Soyuz T-10-1 or Soyuz 7K-ST No.16L).
The crew aboard the spacecraft consisted of Soviet cosmonauts Vladimir Titov and Gennadi Strekalov.
A fire at the base of the rocket burned through the control cables needed to trigger the escape system.
The launch escape system was triggered via a backup radio command sent by ground controllers.
The launch escape tower pulled the crew capsule free of the booster just seconds before the rocket exploded.
The launch vehicle exploded on the launch pad shortly after the crew capsule was pulled clear.
During the rocket-powered escape, the cosmonauts endured extreme accelerations ranging from 14g to nearly 20g.
The crew capsule landed safely about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) from the launch pad.
The cosmonauts survived the launch pad abort in good health despite being badly bruised.
Immediately after the escape system activated, the cosmonauts turned off their cockpit voice recorder to hide their swearing.
Upon meeting the recovery crew, the cosmonauts immediately asked for cigarettes and were given a tumbler of vodka to steady their nerves.
The launch pad fire and explosion debris burned for nearly 20 hours after the accident.
This incident was the only time a crewed launch escape system was fired on the launch pad prior to liftoff.

disputed: The exact acceleration experienced by the crew during escape varies across sources (14-17g in S1 and S2 versus nearly 20g in S4); a script should describe it as extreme forces of 14 to 17g.
The exact seconds between activation and explosion differ (6 seconds in S1/S2, down to 2 to 4 seconds in some accounts mentioned in S2); a script should state 'just seconds before the explosion'.
